Text: What is the normal pulse rate for a neonate, in beats/min? {{c1::100 to 180::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the top of a newborn's normal band is baseline, not distress — a heart rate that would be a serious tachycardia in an adult can be an ordinary finding in a neonate.

Distinguish: the whole neonate band sits above the adult one, so a newborn drifting toward adult-sounding numbers is slowing down rather than settling down.

Text: What is the normal pulse rate for an infant, in beats/min? {{c1::100 to 160::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a pulse of 140 beats/min is a normal infant finding, yet the same rate in a 30-year-old would signal a life-threatening condition — a pulse number means nothing until the patient's age is known.

Cue: an infant is expected to run fast, so tachycardia in an infant is judged against the infant band and never against adult numbers.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal pulse rate for a toddler, in beats/min? {{c1::90 to 150::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the toddler and preschool bands meet at 3 years, so a 3-year-old sits on the boundary between two different normal ranges — settle the age group before calling a pulse fast or slow.

Cue: a slow pulse is the alarming direction in a toddler, because much of the normal adult range falls below a toddler's floor.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal pulse rate for a preschool-age child, in beats/min? {{c1::80 to 140::range}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: preschool age and toddler share one systolic pressure range but not one pulse range, so the two age groups cannot be lumped together for heart rate.

Pitfall: a preschooler's ceiling still reaches well into what would be tachycardia in an adult, so a fast rate in a 4-year-old is measured against the child band.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal pulse rate for a school-age child, in beats/min? {{c1::70 to 120::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a school-age child looks big enough to judge by adult numbers, but the normal pulse band is still faster at the floor and higher at the ceiling than an adult's.

Distinguish: adult pulse values do not arrive until adolescence, and school age runs to 12 years while adolescence begins at 12 — a 12-year-old sits on that boundary.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal pulse rate from adolescence through older adulthood, in beats/min? {{c1::60 to 100::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: an older adult gets no allowance for age — the band that covers a 20-year-old still covers an 80-year-old, so a resting pulse outside it is abnormal however old the patient is.

Distinguish: the pulse band stops changing at adolescence while systolic pressure keeps climbing, so reaching adult heart rate does not mean reaching adult pressure.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate for a neonate, in breaths/min? {{c1::30 to 60::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a newborn's slowest normal breathing is still faster than an adult's fastest normal, so a neonate breathing at an adult rate is in trouble rather than at rest.

Cue: the neonate is the fastest breather of any age group and carries the widest band — a newborn's rate can double and stay inside its own normal.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate for an infant, in breaths/min? {{c1::25 to 50::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: AAOS contradicts itself for the infant — the chapter's narrative calls 60 breaths/min usually normal for an infant, while TABLE 7-1 caps the infant band well below that rate and assigns 60 to a younger age group. Learn the TABLE 7-1 range.

Distinguish: the respiratory band narrows from both ends over the first year, so a rate that is normal for a newborn can already be too fast for a 6-month-old.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate for a toddler, in breaths/min? {{c1::20 to 30::range}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: toddler and preschool age sit side by side with different breathing ranges, so a 3-year-old on the boundary must be assigned to one age group before the rate can be called normal.

Cue: breathing has slowed a long way from infancy by the toddler years, so an infant-speed respiratory rate in a toddler is abnormally fast.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate for a preschool-age child, in breaths/min? {{c1::20 to 25::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the preschool band is one of the narrowest of any age group, so only a few breaths per minute separate normal from abnormal — count the rate rather than estimating it.

Distinguish: preschool age shares a systolic pressure range with the toddler band but keeps its own tighter breathing range, so the age groups do not pair up the same way across the vital signs.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate for a school-age child, in breaths/min? {{c1::15 to 20::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a school-age child breathes close enough to an adult that the band is easy to blur, yet the floor is higher — a rate that is comfortably normal for an adult can be too slow for a 9-year-old.

Cue: judge a school-age rate against the school-age band even when the child is nearly adult-sized, because the criterion is the age group and not body size.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate from adolescence through older adulthood, in breaths/min? {{c1::12 to 20::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: an infant breathing 40 breaths/min is normal, but 40 in an adult is double the top of this band — a respiratory rate means nothing until the patient's age is known.

Distinguish: breathing values stop changing at adolescence and never widen again for age, so an older adult is held to the same range as a young adult.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure for a neonate, in mm Hg? {{c1::50 to 70::range}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: systolic pressure is the one vital sign that climbs with age instead of falling, so the neonate sits at the bottom of the pressure scale while topping the pulse and breathing scales.

Pitfall: a newborn's normal pressure would be profound hypotension in an adult, so a low-looking systolic number is not by itself evidence of shock in a neonate.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure for an infant, in mm Hg? {{c1::70 to 95::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the infant ceiling is the only systolic bound across the age groups that is not a round multiple of ten, and rounding it off changes the number AAOS actually gives.

Distinguish: pressure rises fastest across the first year, so a systolic reading that is normal for a newborn is already too low for a 6-month-old.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure for a toddler or preschool-age child, in mm Hg? {{c1::80 to 100::range}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: toddler and preschool age carry one shared systolic range even though their pulse and breathing ranges differ — pressure is the vital sign where the two age groups merge.

Pitfall: AAOS calls these ranges approximate and notes that they vary between sources, so a reading sitting on a boundary is a number to recheck and trend, not a pass-fail line.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure for a school-age child, in mm Hg? {{c1::80 to 110::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the school-age floor is still below the adolescent floor, so pressure has not finished rising by 12 years — a child this age is not yet held to adult pressure numbers.

Cue: school age is the last childhood band and carries the highest systolic ceiling of the childhood age groups, because the number keeps climbing right through the growth years.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure for an adolescent, in mm Hg? {{c1::90 to 110::range}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: an adolescent reaches adult pulse and breathing values but not adult pressure — the systolic ceiling is still a child's and does not rise until early adulthood.

Distinguish: adolescence borrows the adult pulse and breathing values yet keeps a systolic range of its own, and it is the only age group split that way across the vital signs.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure for an early, middle, or older adult, in mm Hg? {{c1::90 to 130::range}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: systolic pressure is the vital sign that rises with age, and the rise ends at adulthood — one band covers a 20-year-old and an 80-year-old alike.

Pitfall: the life span keeps three separate adult age groups, yet all three share one set of vital sign ranges — the adult divisions matter for risk and disease, not for normal values.

Text: What is the normal body temperature for a neonate? {{c1::98°F to 100°F (37°C to 38°C)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the neonate is the only age group whose normal reaches 100°F (38°C) — a reading that would be a low-grade fever later in life.

Why: a newborn regulates temperature poorly and loses heat fast through a large head and thin skin, so both ends of this band matter.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal body temperature for an infant or toddler? {{c1::96.8°F to 99.6°F (36°C to 37.5°C)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the infant and toddler are the only groups whose normal dips below 98°F, so a reading in the 97s is unremarkable here and would be cool in an adult.

Pitfall: a low reading in a small child is not automatically reassuring — cold stress and sepsis can both drive the temperature down rather than up.

visual_source.note: values read off the extracted TABLE 7-1 plate; the plate is attached to the card as the visual evidence.

Text: What is the normal body temperature from preschool age through older adulthood? {{c1::98.6°F (37°C)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: temperature is the one vital sign that stops changing with age — it settles on a single value from preschool age onward rather than drifting band by band.

Pitfall: an older adult can be seriously infected without a fever, so a normal temperature never rules out sepsis.

Text: Across the life span, the neonate age group covers {{c1::birth to 1 month}}.
Back Extra:
Why: no other phase of life changes as fast as the first year, which is why those 12 months alone carry two names instead of one.

Distinguish: neonate is only the opening slice of that year — a baby stops counting as one long before the first birthday, and the rest of the year belongs to the infant.

Text: Across the life span, the infant age group covers {{c1::1 month to 1 year}}.
Back Extra:
Why: no other phase of life changes as fast as the first year, which is why those 12 months carry two names, and infant is by far the longer of the two.

Pitfall: the band closes at the first birthday, not at a milestone such as walking or talking, so an 11-month-old is still an infant and not yet a toddler.

Text: Across the life span, the toddler age group covers {{c1::1 to 3 years}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: toddler is the first age group whose whole range is stated in years — the two bands before it are still counted in months.

Pitfall: the childhood bands share their boundary years, so a child sitting exactly on either end of this range belongs to two age groups at once.

Text: Across the life span, the preschool age group covers {{c1::3 to 6 years}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the name is the hook — preschool age is the stretch before formal schooling, so the band closes exactly where school age opens.

Ex: a child who has just turned 3 sits in two groups at once, counting as a toddler and as preschool age on the same day.

Text: Across the life span, the school age group covers {{c1::6 to 12 years}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: the boundary years belong to two groups at once — a 12-year-old is school age and an adolescent on the same day.

Cue: the name is the hook — the band opens when formal schooling starts and closes when adolescence begins.

Text: Across the life span, the adolescent age group covers {{c1::12 to 18 years}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: adolescent is the last band that shares a boundary year with a neighbour — from here on the adult bands open a full year after the previous band closes, so no age falls in two of them.

Pitfall: the band runs through the whole of 18, so an 18-year-old is still counted as an adolescent and not yet as an adult.

Text: Across the life span, the early adult age group covers {{c1::19 to 40 years}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the adult bands do not overlap the way the childhood bands do — early adult opens the year after adolescence closes, so no patient is both.

Cue: the band spans more than two decades, so a 20-year-old and a 40-year-old sit in the same group and carry the same expected vital signs.

Text: Across the life span, the middle adult age group covers {{c1::41 to 60 years}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the adult bands butt up against each other without sharing a year, so middle adult starts at 41 and not at 40 — a patient who has just turned 40 is still an early adult.

Cue: all three adult bands carry identical expected vital signs, so middle adult places a patient developmentally rather than promising a different set of numbers.

Back Extra:
Pitfall: the adult bands butt up against each other without sharing a year, so the band opens at 61 and not at 60 — a patient who has just turned 60 is still a middle adult.

Cue: older adult is the only age group left open at the top, so it stretches further than any other band in the life span.

Text: At birth, a neonate usually weighs {{c1::6 to 8 pounds (3 to 3.5 kg)}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the head alone accounts for about 25% of a neonate's birth weight, which is why neonates and infants land headfirst when they fall — carry a high index of suspicion for head and spinal trauma.

Distinguish: 6 to 8 pounds is the weight at birth, before the normal first-week dip, and it stays the baseline that every later growth milestone is measured against.

Text: During the first week of life, a neonate's body weight drops by {{c1::5% to 10%}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the loss is fluid, not a failure to feed, and the neonate starts gaining again in the second week.

Pitfall: the dip is expected rather than alarming — it is the only time in the first year that a healthy baby's weight goes down.

Text: From the second week of life onward, an infant gains about {{c1::1 ounce (30 g) per day}}.
Back Extra:
Why: steady daily gain is what carries an infant to the doubling and tripling milestones of the first year, once the first-week fluid loss has been recovered.

Ex: about 1 ounce a day works out to roughly 2 pounds a month.

Text: An infant doubles his or her birth weight by {{c1::4 to 6 months}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the milestone is a multiple of the birth weight, not of whatever the infant happens to weigh at the time.

Ex: a 7 lb newborn is about 14 lb once the birth weight has doubled.

Text: An infant weighs three times his or her birth weight by {{c1::1 year}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: tripling is measured from the birth weight, not from the already doubled weight, so the second half of the first year adds far less than the first half.

Ex: a 7 lb newborn is about 21 lb at 1 year.
